scenes.headline: Rome ran on flowing water
scenes.narration: Two thousand years ago, Rome delivered fresh water to a huge city with no pumps and no electricity. How? With gravity, patience, and very careful math.

scenes.headline: It all starts at a spring
scenes.narration: Engineers tapped clean springs in the hills, often many miles from the city. The water entered a covered channel and began its slow journey downhill toward Rome.
scenes.body: The first big aqueduct, the Aqua Appia, dates to 312 BC.

scenes.headline: The slope was gentle
scenes.narration: The channel dropped only a tiny amount over each mile. Too steep and the water would erode the stone. Too flat and it would stall. Roman surveyors got it remarkably right.

scenes.headline: Arches carried water over valleys
scenes.narration: When the route crossed a valley, builders raised tall arches to keep the channel at the right height. The famous stacked arches you see in photos are just the visible part.
scenes.body: Most of an aqueduct actually ran underground or at ground level.

media.query: Roman aqueduct arches against a blue sky

scenes.headline: Siphons beat the deepest valleys
scenes.narration: For very deep valleys, Romans sometimes used inverted siphons: sealed pipes that ran down one side and up the other. Pressure pushed the water back up.

scenes.headline: What happened in the city
scenes.narration: Inside Rome, water arrived at distribution tanks and was split between public fountains, baths, and some private homes. Overflow even helped flush the sewers.

scenes.headline: Engineering that outlasted an empire
scenes.narration: Some aqueducts still stand today. Next time you turn on a tap, remember that the idea is Roman: let gravity do the work.
scenes.body: Which ancient invention should we explain next?
